key_insight: In a large academic medical center, AI-related interactions were documented as a real but infrequent clinical phenomenon, often appearing in patients during first psychotic episodes and commonly acting as an amplifier of delusional thinking.
clinical_relevance: For clinicians and researchers, the findings suggest that AI use may worsen or shape psychotic symptoms in vulnerable patients, highlighting the need to ask about conversational AI exposure during psychiatric assessment.
method: EHR keyword search across Vanderbilt University Medical Center records from 12/1/2022 to 4/1/2026
Restricted to records with AI-related content and a primary diagnosis including psychosis
Three raters reviewed notes and classified cases into Catalyst, Amplifier, Co-Author, or Object categories
evidence_signal: The study identified 73 qualifying patients, with 28 rated as AI psychosis and the rest split between neutral AI interactions and AI-themed delusions without documented AI use.
watch_item: Because this was a retrospective single-center EHR study, documentation quality and keyword capture may miss cases or overstate how directly AI caused symptoms.
paper_title: Characterizing artificial intelligence (AI) psychosis in a large academic medical setting: evidence of the new clinical phenomenon and the vulnerability of those in early phases of psychosis
